question: Data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics reveals that around 400 000 tonnes of durum wheat was imported to Italy from Russia between January and November 2023. Over the same period in 2022, around 32 000 tonnes was imported, meaning that there has been an increase of more than 1100 %.

Durum wheat price speculation is now happening in Italy, especially in regions such as Apulia – the Foggia Commodity Exchange reports a drop of EUR 68 per tonne in the last month and a half (February to mid-March 2024) alone for fino, mercantile, buono mercantile and organic durum wheat among other varieties1.
This situation is putting around 200 000 farms at risk and could thus lead to the end of durum wheat production in Italy. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission plan to extend the sanctions to Russian agri-food products to safeguard Italy and Europe’s local production?
Will it implement more transparent policies on markets with import restrictions?
Will it use the CAP’s agricultural reserve fund to mitigate the losses of Italian cereal farmers?
answer: On 22 March 2024, the Commission proposed to increase EU import tariffs on certain cereals, oilseeds, and derived products from Russia and Belarus (2). The proposed measure covers imports of 4.2 million tonnes of products from Russia worth EUR 1.3 billion and includes durum wheat to which the question refers.

The tariff proposed to be applied to imports of durum wheat from Russia and Belarus is believed to be high enough to suppress current imports of the products selected. The proposed measure aims at preventing that Russia redirects significant volumes of grains to the EU market, which could lead to its destabilisation.

The transit of these products from Russia and Belarus via the EU to third countries would be unaffected. The EU remains fully committed to ensuring global food security. The EU policies are fully transparent; the Commission proposal is publicly available and is now discussed by the Member States in view of being adopted by the Council of the European Union.
Prices on the Italian market for durum wheat evolved similarly to those in other Member States, with a general drop observed over the last 2-3 months.

Significant Italian durum wheat imports in 2023/2024 marketing season reflect the low domestic production for two years in a row, which was about 10% lower than a long-term average and even lower than in 2019 and 2020, when Italy also registered a similar level of imports.

Therefore, the current situation cannot be considered as exceptional and as justifying the use of the Common Agricultural Policy agricultural reserve. In parallel, it should be noted that Russia has introduced a temporary ban on exports of durum wheat from December 2023 that is expected to apply until 31 May 2024.
